I am 73 years old. I have walked these fields of Quzhou for 50 years, and I know every low spot where water pools and every corner where the wind cuts hard. My 13.1 mu is not large, but it feeds my household of six. My sons and their wives work in the county town, so it is mostly me and my old woman who tend the land. We have a well, and I am thankful for it because rain on the North China Plain is never certain.

This year, like last year, I will keep 8 mu for the wheat-maize rotation and 5.1 mu for cotton. That is the balance that works. In early October, after the maize comes off, I will run the rotary tiller over the 8 mu and plant improved wheat seed. I spread chicken manure before sowing, then put down compound fertilizer as basal. In spring, when the wheat greens up, I topdress with nitrogen — usually urea or ammonium bicarbonate. I irrigate four times through the season, including a winter irrigation to keep the seedlings from freezing. For pests, I spray four times: twice for insects, once for weeds, and once for rust. If the weather does not betray me, I expect about 450 kg per mu.

The day the wheat is threshed in early June, I plant maize directly into the stubble without tilling. No-tillage saves me time and preserves the soil moisture in the summer heat. I buy Denghai 605 hybrid seed — it is expensive but reliable. One application of compound fertilizer at sowing, two irrigations from the well, and three sprayings for pests. That should give me 500 kg per mu.

The cotton goes on the remaining 5.1 mu. I rotary till in late April and sow improved cotton seed. I apply compound fertilizer and some manure at planting. Cotton is thirsty and delicate — I irrigate three times and spray many times through the season because the bollworms and aphids never give a farmer rest. I expect about 300 kg of seed cotton per mu.

I do not experiment with new methods at my age. I do what my father did, what my neighbors do, and what the land has rewarded for half a century.
